newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian lawyers welcome Singapore verdict.
newsitem.headline: Indian lawyers welcome Singapore verdict.

text.p: Indian lawyers on Thursday cheered a Singapore court decision to award Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and party colleagues $5.65 million in libel damages, saying it was a bold decision which could provide a model.

"It is a very good judgement particularly when a lot of irresponsible criticism or defamation takes place of people in power or position, or those who have acquired some fame," said Duli Chand Singhania, a senior Delhi lawyer.

In a written judgement, the Singapore court ordered Tang Liang Hong, who fled the country after losing in January general elections, to pay the damages to Goh and 10 other members of the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) for calling them liars.
Kapil Sibal, one of India's leading lawyers, said: "I wish courts in India would do that. I wish defamation laws in India were made stronger."
India's free-wheeling press and politicians are often criticised by targets for their strong opinions.
Singhania said he favoured stiff penalties to discourage defamation.
"Under Indian law mostly damages are compensatory and not punitive," Singhania said. "The fear of punishment would be a stronger deterrent."
Sibal is defending former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao against corruption charges, which the Congress party leader has denied.
Singhania is representing Kazakh Airlines in an Indian government inquiry into the world's deadliest mid-air collision last year in which 349 people were killed.
Defamation cases in India are few and can linger on for years before a decision is arrived at, Sibal said.
"A newspaper can publish what it likes, a person can say whatever he feels about another person and the accused person is damned -- damned for life and there is no remedy," said Sibal.
He said a claimant who wins a libel suit is generally awarded a token amount of one, two or 10 rupees -- less than $1.00.
Tavleen Singh, a prominent journalist and political analyst, said Singapore's standards could not prevail in India.
"What a small city state has done would not really be applicable in India," Singh added. India's is the world's second most populous country.
